title: US flights expected to return to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption
text:
US flights expected to return to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption | Lianhe Zaobao 
 Singapore International China Business Opinion Lifestyle Entertainment Search Published / 16 Nov 2026 10:17 S M L XL US flights expected to return to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption
 AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here. 
 The US Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide halt to flight departures on 13 November, causing widespread cancellations and leaving travellers stranded at airports. （Reuters） US flights are expected to return to normal on Monday (16 November) after an air traffic control system failure caused three days of disruption . However, the rare nationwide grounding has exposed ageing US air traffic control infrastructure and sparked recriminations between the two main parties. 
 AFP reported that, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware, as of Sunday (15 November) evening, just over 55 flights to, from and within the US had been cancelled for Monday, far fewer than the more than 1,960 cancellations on Sunday. 
 The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide halt to flight departures on Friday after a failure during an upgrade to communications equipment . 
 US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told ABC on Sunday that although airspace operations were gradually resuming, some aircraft and crew were still not where they were scheduled to be. A full return to normal was therefore not expected until Monday. 
 US President Donald J. Trump addressed the incident for the first time on Sunday, blaming former president Joe Biden’s administration . He accused the previous administration of spending vast sums while leaving an already ageing air traffic control system in even worse shape. He urged Congress to approve funding to modernise the system. 
 Duffy rejected calls to resign over the incident, stressing that he had inherited severely ageing air traffic control infrastructure, with some radar equipment dating back to the 1960s. 
 Sean Duffy has asked Congress for US$50 billion (about S$64 billion) to upgrade the air traffic control system. Democrats countered, however, that Republicans had controlled Congress for the past two years and had already had opportunities to push through the reforms.
